## The whole path

- Hardware (PCB · power · RF) — Boards designed for the enclosure, power budget, and certification lab, not just the bench.

- Firmware (C/C++ · MicroPython) — Firmware that boots safely, recovers from faults, and updates remotely in the field.

- Connectivity (LoRa · BLE · LTE · MQTT) — Radio and protocol architectures for intermittent sites, buffering data locally until the link returns.

- Fleet operations (provisioning · OTA) — Zero-touch provisioning, staged OTA updates with rollback, and remote diagnostics per unit.

- Cloud and data (AWS · serverless · IaC) — Device registries, ingestion pipelines, APIs, and dashboards built as code and sized for the fleet.

- Edge AI (vision · edge models) — Computer vision and inference models running next to the sensor, even when the network drops.

- AI agents (tool servers · audit) — Agents wired to device data and business systems through permissioned, audited tools.

## AI for plant operations, built security-first

Industrial plants already hold the answers to most daily operational questions, split across an ERP, a technical knowledge base, and device telemetry. I originated, designed, and built a serverless AWS tool gateway on the Model Context Protocol that connects AI assistants to all three systems under strict operational security.

Operators, engineers, and managers ask in plain language about machine history, open maintenance tickets, device health, or standard procedures and get answers grounded in real records, with sources named in business terms. Around the gateway sit hybrid keyword-and-semantic search for documentation, daily monitoring summaries, and interfaces built for touch, gloves, and glare on the plant floor.

## How I work

1. Go to the problem. I start from the failing unit, the site, or the log.

2. Instrument it. I make the device and pipeline show what is happening before changing anything.

3. Ship the smallest fix that holds. I deliver the hardware revision, firmware release, or cloud change and validate it on real units.

4. Leave it operable. I hand over runbooks, update paths, and diagnostics so your team owns the system afterwards.

1. Pay on Stripe. Choose your session and pay on Stripe. Use an email address you check. If checkout offers scheduling fields, you can include two preferred times and your time zone.

2. Agree on a time. Within one business day after payment, I’ll email you personally to agree on a time. I coordinate from Colombia (UTC−5). If you didn’t enter your preferences at checkout, reply with them.

4. Get written notes. Within 24 hours after the session, I’ll send written notes with the decisions and next steps.

You can reschedule at no charge up to 24 hours before the session. Reply to the scheduling email. If we can’t agree on a time within seven days after payment, you’ll receive a full refund.

## Frequently asked questions

### How does scheduling work after I pay?

Within one business day after payment, I’ll email you to agree on a time in Colombia time (UTC−5). Once we confirm a time, I’ll send a Google Meet invitation.

### What if we cannot find a mutually convenient time?

If we cannot agree on a time within 7 days of your payment, you receive a full refund via Stripe — no questions asked.

### Can I reschedule my session?

Yes. You can reschedule free of charge up to 24 hours before the confirmed meeting time by replying to our scheduling email.

### What should I prepare or send beforehand?

In your reply, tell me what you need to decide, what you’ve tried and which constraints matter. A redacted schematic, short code excerpt or architecture diagram is usually enough. If you need a non-disclosure agreement (NDA), ask before sending confidential material.

### Can we sign an NDA before sharing proprietary material?

Yes. If your questions involve unreleased hardware, schematics, or proprietary architecture, mention it when we coordinate by email (or message me on LinkedIn before paying) and I will review and sign a standard mutual NDA before the call.

### Will I receive a receipt or invoice for company reimbursement?

If you need a copy of your Stripe receipt, ask when I contact you. If your company needs a particular invoice format or purchase-order reference, contact me on LinkedIn before paying so we can confirm what’s available.

### What do I get after the call?

Within 24 hours after the session, I send concise written notes summarizing the technical tradeoffs discussed, key decisions, and prioritized next steps.

### What if I need an ongoing design review or a multi-week engagement?

See Scoped engagements for the kinds of work I take on. Send the problem, schedule, and constraints on LinkedIn.

### What if I paid and did not hear back within one business day?

Check your spam folder. If the message hasn’t arrived, contact me on LinkedIn with the day and session you bought.

# Underwater ROV Telemetry: Hardware, Firmware, and a Protocol Audit

A degree-project archive brings together custom acquisition boards, embedded firmware and a modern audit of the serial protocol.

<https://ddtdanilo.github.io/work/xsub-telemetry.html>

Early work · 2015–2016

## Project specifications

- MCU — MCF51QE128CLH

- Board — 93.1 × 53.9 mm

- Copper layers — 2

- Footprints — 46

- Named nets — 39

- Track segments — 457

- Vias — 33

## The problem

An underwater remotely operated vehicle (ROV) concentrates every boundary problem found in industrial IoT inside a sealed pressure housing. Sensors on different electrical buses must be sampled reliably, actuator commands must reach thrusters and lighting without jitter, power distribution has to survive inductive motor loads, and a single serial link between the embedded controller and the onboard computer has to carry both telemetry and teleoperation frames cleanly.

Between 2015 and 2016, I designed and validated the telemetry and teleoperation system for **X-Sub**, an underwater robot developed by the Mechatronics Research and Development Group at Universidad Simón Bolívar. The work earned an honorific mention as my undergraduate Electronics Engineering thesis (the full 137-page thesis is preserved in `Libro Tesis.pdf`). Years later, rather than leaving the project as an opaque archive of legacy binaries, I audited the original firmware and hardware files and added modern, dependency-free verification tooling so any engineer can inspect the design honestly.

## System architecture

The archived vehicle architecture splits real-time sensing and actuation from higher-level logging and surface visualization:

- **Embedded controller (`MCU Firmware/X-Sub MCU Firmware/`):** A 32-bit Freescale **MCF51QE128** (ColdFire V1) microcontroller developed in CodeWarrior with Processor Expert drivers and custom C logic in `xSub.c`, `OneWire.c`, and `main.c`.
- **Sensor interfaces:** An **MPU-6050** inertial measurement unit and **HMC6352** digital compass over I²C; a **DS18B20** external temperature sensor over 1-Wire; an **MPX5700AP** pressure sensor and battery-voltage monitoring over ADC; and digital water-presence inputs over GPIO.
- **Actuator outputs:** PWM channels driving four bidirectional brushless ESCs, two pan/tilt camera servos, and two high-intensity LED loads, alongside status and handshake indicators.
- **Custom PCBs (`PCB/`):** Two Altium Designer boards — `X-Sub_Board` for acquisition, control, and sensor interfaces, and `pcDuino Link Board` for power distribution and controller-to-computer interconnection.
- **Onboard and surface path:** The MCF51QE128 exchanges fixed-length binary frames over UART (115200 baud in the Python experiments) with an onboard **pcDuino**, which relays telemetry to surface logging and visualization prototypes originally explored in Python 3.4, LabVIEW, and MATLAB/Simulink.

## Auditing the wire protocol

Re-examining the C source (`xSub.c`, `Events.c`, `Init.c`) a decade later shows both what worked and what would fail a modern production review:

- **Telemetry frames (27 bytes):** Big-endian 16-bit readings covering status, external and internal temperature, external pressure, 3-axis acceleration, 3-axis angular velocity, linear velocity, compass heading, water-presence state, and battery level, ending with a `0xFF` terminator.
- **Command frames (10 bytes):** Four motor setpoints, camera pan and tilt, two light channels, a PC status byte (each 0–255), and a `0xFF` terminator.
- **Documented failure modes:** Although byte 25 of the telemetry frame is named `XOR` in the archived firmware, initialization assigns the fixed decimal constant `26` and no checksum calculation runs during frame assembly. Likewise, the protocol has no framing escape or resynchronization mechanism, no sequence numbers, no command timeout encoded on the wire, and no authentication.

In `docs/PROTOCOL.md` and `docs/HARDWARE.md`, those gaps are documented explicitly instead of glossed over. Any production telemetry link for industrial hardware needs a real CRC, deterministic framing (such as COBS or length-prefixed frames), watchdog fail-safes on command loss, and replay/authentication controls whenever commands cross an untrusted network.

## Modern verification boundary

Legacy CodeWarrior, LabVIEW, and MATLAB binary projects cannot safely be assumed to compile or run unchanged ten years later. The maintained boundary of the repository is therefore deliberately narrow and verifiable:

- `tools/xsub_protocol.py` provides a dependency-free Python 3.11+ CLI to decode 27-byte telemetry frames (reporting raw unsigned integers and offering two's-complement conversion via `signed_16()` without fabricating sensor calibration curves) and encode 10-byte command frames for inspection.
- Automated CI (`quality.yml` and `codeql.yml`) runs Ruff linting, unit tests, and `scripts/verify_repository.py` to validate artifact hashes and repository hygiene, while `docs/HARDWARE.md` lays out a seven-step electrical, DRC/ERC, current-limited bring-up, and recalibration checklist before anyone powers an archived board.

## Takeaway

Good embedded engineering is as much about knowing where a design stops being safe as making it work on the bench. Preserving `X-Sub/Telemetry-System` with an honest protocol audit, explicit safety warnings, and automated verification demonstrates the exact review lens I bring to connected hardware projects today.

## Sources

- [Public repository](https://github.com/X-Sub/Telemetry-System)

- [Hardware guide](https://github.com/X-Sub/Telemetry-System/blob/HEAD/docs/HARDWARE.md)

- [Protocol reference](https://github.com/X-Sub/Telemetry-System/blob/HEAD/docs/PROTOCOL.md)

# Disciplined PCB Component Libraries in Altium Designer

The library pairs automated checks for binary Altium files with a manual review against manufacturer datasheets.

<https://ddtdanilo.github.io/work/altium-pcb-library.html>

Public library · 2019–2026

## Project specifications

- Schematic symbols — 81

- PCB footprints — 106

- Automated CI checks — 6 deterministic checks

- Altium review — 4-part datasheet checklist

- License — CERN-OHL-P-2.0

## The problem

A large share of expensive PCB respins start long before routing: they begin in the component library. One swapped pin on a schematic symbol, a mirrored pin-1 mark, an undersized drill on a power header, or an unverified land pattern pulled from an anonymous forum can turn a two-week fabrication run into scrap hardware.

At the same time, native Altium Designer libraries (`.SchLib` and `.PcbLib`) are opaque binary compound files. Standard `git diff` cannot show whether a footprint pad shifted by 0.2 mm, whether a file was corrupted during a save, or whether temporary Altium history and lock files slipped into a commit.

Over several years of hardware work (2019–2026), I curated my reusable components into `Personal-Altium-Library`, published publicly under CERN-OHL-P-2.0. To make a binary EDA repository trustworthy for both personal reuse and external engineers, I paired the library files with a two-layer validation workflow modeled after software release discipline.

## What the library covers

The repository tracks two checked-in Altium libraries whose exact sizes and SHA-256 digests are recorded in `library-manifest.json`:

- **`AltiumLibraryDDT.SchLib`** (396,800 bytes) — **81 schematic symbols**.
- **`AltiumLibraryDDT.PcbLib`** (36,292,608 bytes) — **106 PCB footprints**.

Across `docs/INVENTORY.md`, the catalog spans practical building blocks from real hardware builds rather than synthetic demo parts: SMD passives across 0402/0603/1206 packages, high-voltage diodes, barrier terminal blocks and shrouded headers, wireless modules (`ESP32-DEVKITC-32D`, `ESP8266_ESP-12`, `HM-10`), power modules (`LM2596`, `MT3608`, `Mini-360`), load-cell and current sensors (`HX711`, `ACS758LCB-050B`), relays (`G5LE`), and micro-SD holders.

## Two-layer validation for binary EDA files

Because CI cannot replace an electrical engineer inspecting copper geometry in Altium, `docs/VALIDATION.md` separates what machines can guarantee from what requires human review in the EDA tool.

### Layer 1: Automated repository integrity (CI)

Running `python3 scripts/validate_repository.py` locally and in GitHub Actions (`quality.yml`) enforces six deterministic checks on every push and pull request:

1. Required project, licensing, and engineering-notice files exist.
2. Both `.SchLib` and `.PcbLib` carry valid compound-file binary signatures (catching truncated or text-corrupted commits immediately).
3. File byte sizes and SHA-256 checksums match `library-manifest.json` exactly.
4. Declared symbol (81) and footprint (106) counts match the tracked inventory in `docs/INVENTORY.md`.
5. Local Markdown documentation links resolve cleanly.
6. Common generated artifacts, Altium backups, and autosave files are blocked from entering Git.

When a component is intentionally added or edited, `scripts/update_manifest.py` refreshes the manifest — and the policy explicitly forbids blindly accepting a regenerated hash without verifying that only intended library entries changed.

### Layer 2: Manual Altium engineering gate

Before any modified symbol or footprint is accepted, `docs/VALIDATION.md` defines a four-part Altium review checklist:

- **Library integrity:** Open and save both libraries without conversion or repair warnings and run built-in library checks.
- **Schematic review:** Verify every pin number, name, electrical type, hidden power pin, designator, and footprint link directly against the current manufacturer datasheet.
- **Footprint review:** Check pad geometry, numbering, drill sizes, thermal pads, solder mask, paste, silkscreen, courtyard, pin-1 indicator, and 3D body height against the manufacturer's recommended land pattern and fabricator tolerances.
- **Integration review:** Place the symbol in a temporary schematic, push it to a temporary PCB, verify all pin-to-pad mappings, run ERC and DRC, and inspect both board sides in 2D and 3D.

## Takeaway

Reliability in connected hardware starts with boring, repeatable habits: versioned manifests, datasheet-first verification, and honest boundaries about what automation can and cannot prove. `Personal-Altium-Library` is both a public engineering resource and a concrete look at how I structure PCB review workflows before releasing Gerbers to fabrication.

## Sources

- [Public repository](https://github.com/ddtdanilo/Personal-Altium-Library)

- [Inventory](https://github.com/ddtdanilo/Personal-Altium-Library/blob/HEAD/docs/INVENTORY.md)

- [Validation guide](https://github.com/ddtdanilo/Personal-Altium-Library/blob/HEAD/docs/VALIDATION.md)

- [Library manifest](https://github.com/ddtdanilo/Personal-Altium-Library/blob/main/library-manifest.json)

# AI for Plant Operations: A Security-First Tool Gateway

Connecting AI assistants to plant ERP records, technical procedures, and device telemetry through a serverless AWS gateway built for least privilege, guarded writes, and full auditability.

<https://ddtdanilo.github.io/work/plant-operations-agents.html>

## The problem on a plant

Running an industrial plant generates operational truth in separate places. The ERP holds sales orders, inventory, manufacturing orders, quality records, maintenance tickets, and equipment history. Standard operating procedures, troubleshooting notes, and wiring references live in a technical knowledge base. Live and historical device telemetry sits in its own monitoring stack.

Routine questions cross all three boundaries at once. An engineer or supervisor wants to know what happened to a specific machine, which maintenance tickets are open at a site, whether a field device is healthy, or what the documented procedure requires. Getting a reliable answer usually means switching portals, piecing together identifiers, or waiting on the one person who knows where a record lives. On the plant floor, the gap is wider because software has to work under touchscreens, gloves, and glare rather than a quiet desk.

Giving an AI assistant direct access to production systems is unacceptable without hard engineering boundaries. Shared credentials hide who acted, the gateway must enforce access, and an unguarded write against an ERP or equipment record can disrupt live operations.

## The design

I originated, designed, and built a single serverless tool gateway on AWS using the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for structured assistant tooling. The gateway routes every tool call to one of three operational domains: the ERP, the technical knowledge base, and live and historical device telemetry.

People ask questions in plain language: what happened to this machine, which tickets are open at this site, whether a device is healthy, or what the procedure states. The assistant queries structured tools behind the gateway, grounds its answer in the actual records, and cites the source in business terms so the reader can verify it immediately.

The gateway sits inside a broader operational workflow designed for daily plant use:

- **Hybrid knowledge search:** The team knowledge base combines keyword search with semantic search, so part numbers, error codes, and natural-language troubleshooting questions all resolve reliably.
- **Daily monitoring summaries:** Automated operational summaries surface recurring issues and fleet health trends without requiring manual checks across every site.
- **Plant-floor interfaces:** Companion interfaces are designed specifically for field conditions, prioritizing large touch targets, glove usability, and legibility under glare.

The gateway verifies identity and permissions, separates reads from guarded writes, and attributes each change to the person who applied it.

## The security model

The gateway infrastructure enforces these controls for every tool call. Every control follows standard least-privilege practice for production enterprise and industrial systems:

- **Per-person identity:** Every user signs in through single sign-on, and access tokens are strictly bound to the gateway as their audience so the token is intended for this service alone.
- **Deny-by-default permissions:** An administrator manages explicit per-person, per-system grants. If a user is not authorized for a given backend or operation, the gateway rejects the call before any downstream request runs.
- **Read and write separation:** Read tools and write tools are explicitly separated in the tool surface, preventing a routine lookup from crossing into a state-changing action.
- **Two-step guarded writes:** Changing a record requires two distinct steps. First, the gateway prepares the exact proposed change for review. Second, the apply step executes only with a signed, expiring token and performs conflict detection to abort if the underlying record changed in the meantime.
- **User-attributed audit ledger:** Every state change is written to an audit ledger under the authenticated person's identity, creating a clear operational trail.
- **Scoped service accounts and managed secrets:** Downstream integrations run with minimum-rights service accounts. Credentials live in a managed secret store and never appear in prompts, tool outputs, or knowledge base documents.
- **Operational limits and observability:** Response-size caps and execution-time limits bound the work each request can trigger, backed by health monitoring, alarms, and usage logs.

### Security controls

- Identity — SSO per person. Gateway-bound tokens.

- Permissions — Deny by default. Grants by person and system.

- Writes — Prepare, then signed apply. Expiry and conflict check.

- Audit — Changes logged under the user’s identity.

- Secrets — Managed store. Kept out of prompts and documents.

- Limits — Response-size and time caps.

- Monitoring — Health checks, alarms, and usage logs.

## What it changed for the team

With one controlled entry point over operational records, operators, engineers, and managers spend less time hunting across disconnected interfaces and more time acting on verified facts. Questions about machine history, open tickets, device status, and documented procedures receive grounded answers with clear business sources instead of tribal knowledge or guesswork.

Just as important, separating reads from two-step guarded writes lets teams move past read-only demos into real operational workflows. People can prepare updates with confidence that concurrent changes are caught, permissions are enforced, and every action is attributable to the person who approved it.

## What I would bring to yours

If your industrial, hardware, or operations team wants AI connected to ERP records, internal documentation, or device telemetry without compromising production security, I can design and build the same pattern for your environment. That covers the Model Context Protocol gateway on AWS, identity and per-system authorization, two-step write guards and audit logging, hybrid knowledge search, and interfaces usable on the floor.

Start with a focused architecture session or reach out on LinkedIn to scope a dedicated build.
